analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to sell parts, tools, and manuals to independent repair shops and owners.
analysis.headline: The Fair Repair Act, introduced February 5, 2026 with two cosponsors, sits in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require makers of digital electronic equipment — phones, laptops, appliances, and similar products — to sell repair parts, tools, and documentation to independent repair shops and device owners on terms no worse than they give their own authorized repair networks. It would also ban "parts pairing," the software practice of rejecting or degrading third-party replacement parts and flashing warning messages about them. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of electronics — households that would otherwise pay manufacturer-set repair prices or replace devices outright — plus independent repair shops, which gain access to the same parts, tools, and manuals that authorized networks get. Cheaper repairs also mean devices stay in use longer, cutting e-waste.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: OEMs must make documentation, parts, and tools available to independent repair providers and owners on terms equivalent to the best terms they offer their own authorized repair networks, including software updates.

The bill bans parts pairing and similar mechanisms that block functional third-party parts, degrade device performance after an independent repair, display non-dismissible warnings about non-manufacturer parts, or limit who can buy parts or perform repairs.

If a device has a security lock, the manufacturer must provide what is needed to disable and reset it during repair, so security features cannot be used to lock owners out of fixing their own property.
Both the FTC and state attorneys general can enforce the requirements, with states able to seek penalties, damages, and restitution for their residents.

analysis.who_pays: Electronics manufacturers, who would lose pricing power over repair parts and services, and their authorized repair networks, which would no longer be the exclusive channel for parts and repairs. Some of that cost could be passed to buyers through higher device prices, though repair competition would push the other way.
analysis.who_pays_short: Electronics manufacturers and their authorized repair networks

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly exempts motor vehicles, motor vehicle equipment, medical devices, off-road and non-road vehicles (including aircraft, motorcycles, boats, and ATVs), and safety communications equipment, so repair restrictions on those products — including hospital equipment and farm-adjacent machinery — would be untouched.

Manufacturers are freed from liability for damage, data loss, privacy breaches, or improper use of personal data arising from repairs done by independent shops or owners, shifting the risk of a bad repair onto the person who chose it.
Requiring manufacturers to hand over tools that disable security locks, even with reset requirements, draws a good-faith objection that wider access to security-critical tools could be abused.

The trade-secret carve-out — manufacturers need not divulge trade secrets beyond what is necessary to supply parts, tools, and documentation — leaves room for disputes over what must actually be shared.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and straightforward: people who own a device would be able to fix it — or have it fixed affordably — instead of being steered into manufacturer-priced repairs or forced replacement. The honest costs are the liability shield for manufacturers and the risk questions around security-lock tools, both of which fall on the repair side rather than the manufacturer side. The biggest design weakness is what was left out: cars, medical devices, and most vehicles are exempt, so the bill covers consumer electronics but not the categories where repair restrictions most often strand people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 5, 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Morelle (D-NY), joined by Ms. Perez, introduced the Fair Repair Act in the House on February 5, 2026.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which has jurisdiction over consumer protection matters.
The bill has two cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, device manufacturers — they keep the current repair restrictions and pricing power, because the bill has not advanced anywhere it could become law.

for.name: Rep. Joseph Morelle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Repair Act and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — since it was referred on February 5, 2026.

against.name: Consumer electronics manufacturers
against.role: Major device makers (Apple, Samsung, and peers)
against.what_they_did: Have a long, well-documented record of opposing right-to-repair legislation at the state and federal level, fighting mandates to share parts, tools, and diagnostic software.

sides.party_line_note: The only support on record is two Democratic cosponsors with no votes or public Republican positions, so the partisan shape is not yet established.

industries.note: The bill forces them to sell parts, tools, and repair documentation at their best authorized-repair terms and bans parts pairing that rejects or degrades third-party parts, cutting into high-margin repair and parts revenue and weakening the pressure to replace rather than repair devices.
They get guaranteed access to the same parts, tools, manuals, and updates as manufacturer-authorized networks, and are freed from warning-message workarounds for third-party parts.
They lose their exclusive position as the channel with full parts and tool access, though the bill leaves their warranty and recall arrangements with OEMs intact.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle, medical device, and off-road vehicle makers
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts them, leaving their existing repair restrictions — dealership service monopolies, locked-down medical equipment — fully in place.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors, no committee action, and no hearing scheduled, the likely path is that the bill stalls in the Energy and Commerce Committee and never reaches a House vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027 — the fate of most right-to-repair bills in Washington, even as states keep passing their own repair laws.
